L341: ## Appendix A Related Work
L342: ### A.1 Reinforcement Learning and Entropy in Large Language Models
L343: Inspired by DeepSeek-R1 (cite44†Guo et al., 2025 ), RLVR has been extensively adopted in the post-training of LLMs, yielding a series of notable contributions (cite113†Wen et al., 2025 ; cite114†Huang et al., 2025 ; cite115†Cheng et al., 2025b ; cite116†Chen et al., 2025 ). Despite the remarkable success of RLVR, a growing body of literature identifies entropy collapse as a critical challenge within this paradigm (cite51†Cui et al., 2025 ; cite52†Shen, 2025 ).
L344: Specifically, (cite51†Cui et al., 2025 ) analyzes policy entropy collapse as a major obstacle in scaling RL for LLM reasoning and proposes mechanisms to overcome it, while further elucidating the relationship between policy entropy and model performance. Meanwhile, (cite117†Wang et al., 2025b ) demonstrate that performing policy gradient updates exclusively on high-entropy tokens can more efficiently enhance model performance—an effect that is particularly pronounced in larger models.
L345: Furthermore, through theoretical analysis, (cite52†Shen, 2025 ) establish that entropy collapse severely compromises output diversity; this restricts the gradients available for continuous training, ultimately leading to a degradation in final performance. Finally, (cite118†Jin et al., 2026 ) delineate the key factors governing entropy dynamics, including the clipping threshold, the number of offline updates, and the diversity of training data.
L346: ### A.2 Control of Entropy in Large Language Models
L347: Entropy is often a critical metric in RL for LLMs. To mitigate the phenomenon of entropy collapse during the RL process, numerous studies have optimized and improved the framework across multiple dimensions. In traditional approaches (cite56†Schulman et al., 2017 ; cite119†Ziebart et al., 2008 ), entropy maximization is employed by introducing an entropy regularization term into the loss function to prevent a continuous decline in entropy during training.
L348: Specifically, (cite56†Schulman et al., 2017 ) incorporated entropy regularization into the PPO algorithm to maintain policy exploration. However, literature suggests that this regularization method is not consistently effective in large language models; (cite52†Shen, 2025 ) elucidates the reasons behind this inefficacy.
L349: In the context of preventing entropy collapse during model training, DAPO (cite54†Yu et al., 2025 ) was the first to propose the “Clip-Higher” strategy. They argue that the original upper clipping threshold truncation restricts the probability increase of low-probability tokens to some extent, thereby limiting the diversity of model generation.
L350: Consequently, they employ a larger upper clipping threshold for the importance ratio to avoid clipping low-probability tokens, resulting in a degree of entropy increase. TDPO (cite58†Wang et al., 2025a ) differentiates the clipping range at the token dimension; building on the DAPO approach, it restricts the upper clipping threshold for high-probability tokens in positive samples while extending the lower clipping threshold for low-probability tokens.
L351: CISPO (cite57†MiniMax et al., 2025 ) does not directly mask tokens during the clipping process but retains their gradients to ensure continued participation in training, uniformly clamping only the out-of-range importance weights to predefined upper and lower bounds. Clip-Cov (cite51†Cui et al., 2025 ) restricts token updates by randomly selecting a small subset of tokens with high covariance and either detaching their gradients or applying a KL penalty during the policy gradient update.
L352: SAPO (cite72†Gao et al., 2025 ) replaces hard clipping with a temperature-controlled smooth gating mechanism to construct a continuous trust region. Although these works attempt to control entropy by manipulating the clipping threshold, they lack a systematic understanding of how the clipping threshold regulates entropy and exhibit limited flexibility.
L353: ## Appendix B Theoretical Proofs
L354: 
L355: Here, we mainly conduct detailed proof and derivation for the two conclusions cite67†Section B.1 and cite73†Equation 10 in the article.
L356: ### B.1 Proof of cite67†Section B.1 L357: 
L358: cite67†Section B.1 : The inner product between the objective gradient $\nabla_{z}L$ and the global entropy gradient $\nabla_{z}H$ is:
L359:  | $\displaystyle\langle\nabla_{z}L,$  | $\displaystyle\nabla_{z}H\rangle\propto\hat{A}(\mathbf{e}_{a}-\mathbf{p})^{\top}\left[-\mathbf{p}\odot(\ln\mathbf{p}+H\cdot\mathbf{1})\right]$  |
L360:  |  | $\displaystyle=-\hat{A}\left[\underbrace{p_{a}(\ln p_{a}+H)}_{\text{Token-specific term}}-\underbrace{\sum_{x\in V}p_{x}^{2}(\ln p_{x}+H)}_{\text{Global baseline term}}\right]$  |
L361: Proof. Let $V$ be the vocabulary set. For a given state, let $\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|}$ denote the logits output by the network. The policy distribution $\mathbf{p}=\text{softmax}(\mathbf{z})$ is defined such that for any token $x\in V$:
L362: 
L363:  | $$p_{x}=\frac{e^{z_{x}}}{\sum_{k\in V}e^{z_{k}}}$$  |
L364: 
L365: The entropy of the policy is defined as:
L366: 
L367:  | $$H(\mathbf{p})=-\sum_{x\in V}p_{x}\ln p_{x}$$  |
L368: To compute gradients with respect to logits $z$, we first establish the partial derivative of the probability $p_{x}$ with respect to the logit $z_{y}$:
L369: 
L370:  | $$\frac{\partial p_{x}}{\partial z_{y}}=p_{x}(\delta_{xy}-p_{y})=\begin{cases}p_{x}(1-p_{x})&\text{if }x=y\\
L371: -p_{x}p_{y}&\text{if }x\neq y\end{cases}$$  |
L372: 
L373: where $\delta_{xy}$ is the Kronecker delta. We apply the chain rule to find the gradient of entropy $H$ with respect to a specific logit $z_{y}$:
L374:  | $$\frac{\partial H}{\partial z_{y}}=\sum_{x\in V}\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_{x}}\frac{\partial p_{x}}{\partial z_{y}}$$  |
L375: 
L376: First, the derivative of entropy with respect to probability $p_{x}$ is:
L377: 
L378:  | $$\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_{x}}=-\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{x}}(p_{x}\ln p_{x})=-(1+\ln p_{x})$$  |
L379: 
L380: Substituting this and the softmax Jacobian into the chain rule summation:
L381: 
L382:  | $$\frac{\partial H}{\partial z_{y}}=\sum_{x\in V}-(1+\ln p_{x})\cdot p_{x}(\delta_{xy}-p_{y})$$  |
L383: Distributing the terms:
L384: 
L385:  | $\displaystyle\frac{\partial H}{\partial z_{y}}$  | $\displaystyle=-\left[\sum_{x\in V}(1+\ln p_{x})p_{x}\delta_{xy}-\sum_{x\in V}(1+\ln p_{x})p_{x}p_{y}\right]$  |
L386:  |  | $\displaystyle=-\left[p_{y}(1+\ln p_{y})-p_{y}\sum_{x\in V}p_{x}(1+\ln p_{x})\right]$  |
L387: 
L388: Expanding the summation $\sum p_{x}(1+\ln p_{x})=\sum p_{x}+\sum p_{x}\ln p_{x}$.
L389:  | $\displaystyle\frac{\partial H}{\partial z_{y}}$  | $\displaystyle=-\left[p_{y}+p_{y}\ln p_{y}-p_{y}(1-H)\right]$  |
L390:  |  | $\displaystyle=-\left[p_{y}+p_{y}\ln p_{y}-p_{y}+p_{y}H\right]$  |
L391:  |  | $\displaystyle=-p_{y}(\ln p_{y}+H)$  |
L392: 
L393: Expressing this in vector notation yields the result provided in your text:
L394: 
L395:  | $$\nabla_{z}H=-\mathbf{p}\odot(\ln\mathbf{p}+H\cdot\mathbf{1})$$  |
L396: The standard Policy Gradient loss for a selected action $a$ is $L(\theta)\approx\hat{A}\ln p_{a}$. The gradient with respect to logits is a known standard result involving the one-hot vector $\mathbf{e}_{a}$:
L397: 
L398:  | $$\nabla_{z}L=\hat{A}(\mathbf{e}_{a}-\mathbf{p})$$  |
L399: 
L400: We now compute the dot product between the two gradients derived above. This metric indicates alignment between the learning signal and the direction of entropy growth.
L401:  | $\displaystyle\langle\nabla_{z}L,\nabla_{z}H\rangle$  | $\displaystyle=\left(\hat{A}(\mathbf{e}_{a}-\mathbf{p})\right)^{\top}\left(-\mathbf{p}\odot(\ln\mathbf{p}+H\cdot\mathbf{1})\right)$  |
L402:  |  | $\displaystyle=-\hat{A}(\mathbf{e}_{a}-\mathbf{p})^{\top}\left(\mathbf{p}\odot(\ln\mathbf{p}+H\cdot\mathbf{1})\right)$  |
L403:  |  | $\displaystyle=-\hat{A}\left[p_{a}(\ln p_{a}+H)-\sum_{x\in V}p_{x}^{2}(\ln p_{x}+H)\right]$  |
L404: ### B.2 Proof of cite73†Equation 10 L405: 
L406: cite73†Equation 10 : Considering the gradient of the objective for a specific sampled token $a$ with respect to the logit of a generic token $x$ (denoted as $z_{x}$):
L407:  | $$\begin{split}\frac{\partial(\ln\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)\cdot\hat{A})}{\partial z_{x}}&=\frac{\partial\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)}{\partial z_{x}}\cdot\frac{\hat{A}}{\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)}\\
L408: &\hskip-50.0pt=\begin{cases}(1-\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s))\cdot\hat{A}&\text{if }x=a\\
L409: -\pi_{\theta}(x\mid s)\cdot\hat{A}&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\end{split}$$  |  | (10)
L410: 
L411: Proof adapted from (cite72†Gao et al., 2025 ).
L412:  | $\displaystyle\frac{\partial(\ln\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)\cdot\hat{A})}{\partial z_{x}}$  | $\displaystyle=\frac{\partial\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)}{\partial z_{x}}\cdot\frac{\hat{A}}{\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)}$  |
L413:  |  | $\displaystyle=\frac{\mathds{1}(x=a)\exp(z_{a})\sum_{x^{\prime}}\exp(z_{x^{\prime}})-\exp(z_{a})\exp(z_{x})}{\left(\sum_{x^{\prime}}\exp(z_{x^{\prime}})\right)^{2}}\cdot\frac{\hat{A}}{\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)}$  |
L414:  |  | $\displaystyle=\begin{cases}(1-\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s))\cdot\hat{A}&\text{if }x=a\qquad\text{sampled token}\\
L415: -\pi_{\theta}(x\mid s)\cdot\hat{A}&\text{otherwise}\qquad\text{unsampled token}\end{cases}$  |
L416: ## Appendix C Experimental Setup
L417: ### C.1 Models and Datasets
L418: In the preliminary exploration experiments, we used the Qwen2.5-Math-7B model. In the benchmark evaluation experiments, we utilized Qwen2.5-Math-7B and Qwen2.5-7B as the base policy model. The model is trained using the DAPO-Math-17k dataset.
L419: For evaluation and validation, we primarily report performance on the AIME24 (cite81†Zhang and Math-AI, 2024 ), AIME25 (cite82†Zhang and Math-AI, 2025 ), AMC (cite84†Lightman et al., 2023 ), MATH-500 (cite84†Lightman et al., 2023 ), GSM8k (cite83†Cobbe et al., 2021 ), and Olympiad (cite84†Lightman et al., 2023 ) benchmark. To support complex reasoning tasks, we configure the maximum sequence lengths 4096 tokens for Qwen2.5-Math-7B and 8192 tokens for Qwen2.5-7B.
L420: ### C.2 Training Configuration
L421: 
L422: We employ GRPO as the advantage estimator. The model is trained for a total of 400 steps with a global batch size of 512. During the rollout phase, we sample $N=8$ responses per prompt to estimate the baseline and advantages. The optimization uses the AdamW optimizer with the following hyperparameters:

L425: 
L426: Learning Rate: $1\times 10^{-6}$.
L427: 
L428:   * •
L429: 
L430: Weight Decay: 0.1.
L431: 
L432:   * •
L433: 
L434: Gradient Clipping: 1.0.
L435: 
L436:   * •
L437: KL penalty coefficient: The KL penalty coefficient ($\beta_{KL}$) is set to 0.0.
L438: For the dynamic linear parameters of the upper clipping threshold and lower clipping threshold, we calibrated the upper clipping threshold to exceed $\epsilon_{high}$ in the low-probability regime while remaining lower in the high-probability regime (the same applies to the lower clipping threshold). The linear slope and intercept of the dynamic upper clipping threshold are set to $-0.25$ and $0.5$, and the linear slope and intercept of the dynamic lower clipping threshold are set to $-0.13$ and $0.3$.
L439: Experiments have shown that this setting has extensive generalization ability.

L441: 
L442: Experiments are conducted on a single node equipped with 8 $\times$ H100 GPUs. To maximize training throughput and memory efficiency, we implement a hybrid parallelism strategy using the verl (cite120†Sheng et al., 2024 ) framework:

L446: Inference: We utilize the vLLM (cite121†Kwon et al., 2023 ) engine with a tensor model parallelism size of 4. We employ a sampling temperature of 1.0 and Top-$p=1.0$.
L447:

L449: Training: The actor model is trained using Fully Sharded Data Parallel with parameter and optimizer offloading enabled. We additionally utilize Ulysses sequence parallelism with a size of 4.

L493: ## Appendix E Other Experimental Results
L494: ### E.1 Analysis of the Curves of Entropy and Avg Clipping Threshold
L495: 
L496: We have saved the entropy and the Avg Clipping threshold curves during the training process of the Dynamic Clipping Lower threshold, Dynamic Clipping Upper threshold, Ours-ID, Ours-DID, and Ours-OD methods for Qwen2.5-Math-7B. As shown in cite126†Figure 10 , the entropy and the Avg Clipping threshold curves during the training process of the Ours-ID, Ours-DID, and Ours-OD methods for Qwen2.5-7B are presented in cite127†Figure 11 .
L497: It can be seen that when the model’s average clipping upper threshold is larger, the entropy of the model tends to be in an increasing state, and when the clipping upper threshold decreases and the clipping lower threshold also decreases, the model’s entropy is in a decreasing state. This also verifies the effectiveness of our adjustment mechanism.

L499: ### E.2 Analysis of Clipping Probability Curve
L500: 
L501: Figure 12: Graph of Model Entropy and Average Token Clipping Probability
L502: 
L503: The clipping probability of the model refers to the proportion of tokens that are clipped during the model’s training process. This proportion reflects the number of tokens affected by the clipping mechanism during the model’s training.
L504: As can be seen from cite128†Figure 12 , our entropy control strategy is effectively reflected in the clipping ratio during the model’s training process. For example, in the early stages of training, the token clipping probability of the Ours-ID method is low, and at this time, the entropy is in a period of increase. In the later stages of training, the token clipping probability of the Ours-ID method is high, and at this time, it is in a period of entropy decrease.
L505: In the Ours-OD method, this characteristic is reflected in the fact that the entropy also fluctuates throughout the training process.
L506: ### E.3 Experiment on Replacing Dynamic Clipping Threshold with Clip-Higher and Clip-Lower
L507: 
L508: If we do not use Dynamic upper Clipping Threshold and Dynamic lower Clipping Threshold, but instead use Clip-Higher and Clip-Lower as the adjustment mechanism for entropy increase and decrease, and apply them to the entropy control strategy in our cite15†Section 4.2 , the final results are shown in cite129†Figure 13 .
L509: We can see that although Clip-Higher and Clip-Lower are effective means of controlling entropy increase and decrease, they may affect the performance of the model because they adopt a one-size-fits-all approach to tokens in different regions without dynamic adjustment. On the other hand, the entropy increase and decrease of the model cannot be effectively and precisely controlled by Clip-Higher and Clip-Lower, and we fail to observe the Increase-Decrease or Decrease-Increase-Decrease of Entropy.
L510: It still faces the problem of entropy collapse.
